title: Uthman's copies
hook: the caliph Uthman has standard copies sent to the cities

segments.voice: Yesterday, Abu Bakr's collection: Zayd gathering the Qur'an into one set of sheets, kept in the end by Hafsah. Your line was gathered. Day three hundred seventeen.

In the time of the caliph Uthman, a commander named Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman came back from a campaign far to the north, in Armenia and Azerbaijan. What alarmed him there wasn't the fighting. Soldiers from Syria and soldiers from Iraq had been reciting the Qur'an differently from one another, and quarreling about it, each side sure the other was wrong. He went straight to Uthman in Medina.
screen: `A COMMANDER COMES HOME WORRIED.` → `TWO ARMIES, TWO WAYS OF RECITING.` → `STRAIGHT TO UTHMAN.`

segments.voice: Hudhayfah's plea, as Bukhari records it, was this: rescue this community before they differ over the Book the way earlier peoples differed. Uthman acted. He sent to Hafsah for the sheets gathered under Abu Bakr, and set Zayd ibn Thabit to work again, now with three men of Quraysh. His instruction: where you differ with Zayd over how to write a word, write it in the dialect of Quraysh, because the Qur'an came down in their tongue. They made copies, and Uthman sent one to each of the main cities, such as Kufa, Basra and Damascus, and kept one in Medina. Reports differ on how many: four, five, seven. He returned the sheets to Hafsah and ordered other personal copies burned, so there would be one standard. That was hard for some. Abdullah ibn Mas'ud was unhappy at first about giving up his own copy. Yet over time the companions accepted Uthman's text, and Ali is reported to have said he would have done the same. The word for such a copy is mushaf, from sahifah, a sheet: the bound, written Qur'an, the thing on the shelf. Muslims today say the text in every mushaf follows Uthman's copies, and its spelling is called the Uthmani script. Tradition links some very old copies, kept today in places like Istanbul and Tashkent, to Uthman's time; researchers debate their dates.
screen: `HUDHAYFAH'S ALARM` · `ZAYD AND THREE MEN OF QURAYSH` · `A COPY FOR EACH CITY` · `MUSHAF: THE WRITTEN COPY`

segments.voice: Bring an early copy to mind: brown parchment, long slanting letters, carried by camel to a far city, set down in a mosque and read aloud to people who never met the Prophet. Then let the same words reach you, here, today, and breathe with that distance.
Mushaf. A written, bound copy of the Qur'an, from sahifah, a sheet. Muslims hold that every mushaf today follows the text of Uthman's copies. Today's word.
Your line: one text, many cities. The same words, from Medina to wherever you are. See you tomorrow.

howItsDone: Muslims read from a mushaf whose text follows the copies Uthman sent to the cities, and printed copies usually note that they follow the Uthmani script.

chat.says: Why did Uthman have official copies of the Qur'an made and sent out?
options: Soldiers were reciting differently and quarreling, so he sent one standard copy to each main city.
The old sheets had been lost, so Zayd rewrote the Qur'an from his own memory alone.
Each city wanted its own local version, so he made a different copy for every one.
chat.meaning: Hudhayfah warned of quarrels over recitation. Uthman had copies made from Hafsah's sheets and sent one standard to each main city.

mushaf.meaning: a written, bound copy of the Qur'an

Uthman.meaning: the caliph who sent standard copies to the cities

Hudhayfah.meaning: a commander alarmed by quarrels over recitation

Quraysh.meaning: the tribe whose dialect the copies followed

Uthmani.meaning: the spelling of the Qur'an that follows Uthman's copies

sahifah.meaning: a sheet; the word mushaf comes from it

sources.ref: Sahih al-Bukhari 4987 (Hudhayfah's alarm; Uthman's copies; the dialect of Quraysh)

notes: Bukhari 4987 details paraphrased from memory; confirm. The three Qurashi scribes (Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr, Sa'id ibn al-As, Abd al-Rahman ibn al-Harith) are not named in the voice.
Date: about 25 AH / c. 650 CE ('about twenty years after'); confirm.
Cities receiving copies and the number of copies vary by report; confirm the examples.
Ali's reported approval (Ibn Abi Dawud) and Ibn Mas'ud's initial objection: confirm framing.

Manuscripts: the Topkapi (Istanbul), Tashkent (Samarkand) and Cairo (al-Husayni) copies are traditionally associated with Uthman; many researchers date them to the late 7th–8th centuries. Early fragments (e.g. Birmingham) have been radiocarbon-dated to the 7th century. Confirm wording.
